blocks.text: Feature Transformation taught you how to reshape the distribution of a single column, fixing skew with a log transform or putting a column on a friendlier scale. This lesson is a completely different kind of transformation. It has nothing to do with statistics or distributions at all. It is about format. At the very end of every preprocessing pipeline, no matter how clean and well engineered your DataFrame is, a model does not train on a DataFrame. It trains on plain NumPy arrays, split into a specific shape, arranged in a specific way. This lesson is about that final structural step, turning a finished DataFrame into the exact array shapes a model actually consumes.

blocks.caption: The whole lesson in one picture, DataFrame in, model ready arrays out.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706350-900607642.png
1. Introduction

Every tutorial you have ever seen ends with a line that looks roughly like model.fit(X, y). Almost nobody stops to explain where X and y actually come from, or why X always seems to need two dimensions even when you are only feeding it one column. That gap is exactly what this lesson closes. You already know how to clean a DataFrame, engineer new columns, and fix skewed distributions. What is left is the handoff, the moment your tidy DataFrame stops being a DataFrame and becomes the raw arrays scikit-learn, PyTorch, or TensorFlow actually expect.

None of this is difficult once you see it laid out, but nearly every beginner trips over at least one part of it, usually the reshape step. By the end of this lesson you will be able to take any preprocessed DataFrame and produce exactly the arrays a model wants, with the right dtype, the right dimensions, and the right shape, every time.

blocks.text: 2. From DataFrame to NumPy Array

A pandas DataFrame is already built on top of NumPy under the hood, each column is stored as a block of array data with an index and column labels wrapped around it. Converting a DataFrame to a plain NumPy array mostly just means stripping that wrapper away and keeping the raw numbers. There have long been two ways to do this, the older .values attribute and the newer .to_numpy() method, and picking between them is worth understanding properly rather than just copying whichever one shows up first in a tutorial.
2.1 .values Versus .to_numpy()

.values has been part of pandas from very early on. It is a plain attribute, not a method, meaning you access it without parentheses and without being able to pass it any arguments at all. It simply hands you back whatever internal array representation the DataFrame happens to be using.

.to_numpy() is newer and was added specifically to give you an explicit, well documented, and more predictable way to do the exact same conversion. It is a method, so it takes real arguments, you can pass it a dtype to control the output type, a copy flag to control whether it duplicates the underlying data, and even an na_value to control how missing values get represented.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "sqft": [1200, 1450, 900],
    "bedrooms": [3, 3, 2],
})

arr_values = df.values
arr_to_numpy = df.to_numpy(dtype="float64", copy=True)

print(type(arr_values), type(arr_to_numpy))
# both are numpy.ndarray here, this simple case behaves identically either way

blocks.caption: Same DataFrame, two access paths, only one of them guarantees a real ndarray back.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706350-521413430.png

blocks.title: Where .values genuinely gets confusing
blocks.content: On a plain DataFrame of ordinary numeric or string columns, .values and .to_numpy() behave the same. The real difference shows up with pandas extension dtypes. A categorical column accessed through .values can hand you back a pandas Categorical object instead of a plain ndarray, which quietly breaks code that assumes it has a real NumPy array to call .reshape() or .mean() on. A timezone aware datetime column accessed through .values silently converts to naive UTC values, dropping the timezone with no warning. .to_numpy() is guaranteed to always return a genuine numpy.ndarray, and its explicit dtype argument lets you control conversions like this on purpose instead of by accident.

blocks.text: 2.2 Why .to_numpy() Is Now the Recommended Choice

Put together, this is why the pandas documentation itself recommends reaching for .to_numpy() instead of .values in new code. It is not that .values is broken or about to disappear, plenty of existing code still uses it fine. It is that .to_numpy() is explicit about what you are asking for, accepts arguments so you can control dtype and copy behavior on purpose, and is guaranteed to return a real ndarray every single time regardless of what unusual dtype a column happens to hold.

blocks.alt: Why .to_numpy Is Now the Recommended Choice
blocks.caption: The exact two edge cases that make .values unpredictable in practice.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706351-286138554.png

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect",".values",".to_numpy()"],"rows":[["What it is","A plain attribute, no arguments accepted","A method, accepts dtype, copy, and na_value arguments"],["Extension dtypes like Categorical","Can return the extension type itself, not a plain ndarray","Always returns a genuine numpy.ndarray"],["Timezone aware datetime columns","Silently converts to naive UTC, dropping timezone info","Same default behavior, but you can request dtype=object to keep full Timestamp objects"],["Pandas team guidance","Considered the older, less explicit option","Actively recommended in current pandas documentation"]]}

blocks.title: The practical rule
blocks.content: Default to .to_numpy() in every new script you write. Reach for .values only if you are reading old code that already uses it. For the plain numeric DataFrames you will build in the rest of this lesson, the two produce identical output, so the choice here is really about writing code that stays predictable as your DataFrames grow more columns and more dtypes over time.

blocks.text: 3. Splitting Features From the Target: X and y

Once your DataFrame is fully preprocessed, every value cleaned, encoded, and scaled the way you want, the very next thing every supervised learning workflow needs is a split into two pieces. One piece holds everything the model is allowed to look at, called X. The other piece holds the single thing the model is trying to predict, called y. This split shows up identically whether you are predicting house prices, classifying emails as spam, or forecasting tomorrow demand, the names X and y are close to universal across the entire ML ecosystem.

blocks.alt: Splitting Features From the Target: X and y
blocks.caption: Same DataFrame, two arrays, two different jobs.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706351-883628986.png
3.1 What X and y Actually Represent

X is a 2D array, shaped n_samples by n_features. Every row is one example, a single house, a single email, a single customer. Every column is one feature describing that example, square footage, word count, days since last purchase. y is a 1D array, shaped just n_samples, one value per example, the label or target you are trying to predict for that row and nothing else.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "sqft": [1200, 1450, 900, 1600],
    "bedrooms": [3, 3, 2, 4],
    "distance_to_city_km": [5.2, 12.8, 3.1, 20.4],
    "price": [62, 71, 48, 88],
})

feature_cols = ["sqft", "bedrooms", "distance_to_city_km"]
X = df[feature_cols].to_numpy()
y = df["price"].to_numpy()

print(X.shape)   # (4, 3)  four rows, three feature columns
print(y.shape)   # (4,)    four target values, one per row

items: Predicting house price, X holds sqft, bedrooms, and distance to city, y holds price
Classifying an email as spam, X holds word counts and sender features, y holds the spam or not spam label
Forecasting demand, X holds past sales and calendar features, y holds tomorrow demand

blocks.text: 3.2 A Shape Level Split, Not a Row Level Split

It matters a lot to keep this X and y split conceptually separate from the train and test split you are about to learn in the very next lesson. The X and y split happens along columns. You are deciding which columns are inputs and which single column is the answer. Every row of the DataFrame is still present in both X and y, nothing gets dropped, nothing gets set aside. The train and test split, by contrast, happens along rows. It takes the X and y you already built here and divides their rows into a group the model learns from and a group held back to check how well it actually learned.

blocks.alt: A Shape Level Split, Not a Row Level Split
blocks.caption: Columns first, rows second, and the order genuinely matters.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706351-572311905.png

blocks.title: Why the order matters
blocks.content: X and y always come first because train and test splitting operates on X and y as its input, not on the raw DataFrame. You will see in the Dataset Splitting lesson right after this one that a function like train_test_split takes X and y as arguments and returns four pieces, X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test. None of that is possible until X and y already exist as clean, separate arrays, which is exactly what this section just built.

blocks.text: 4. The Shape Every ML Library Expects

Libraries like scikit-learn are not flexible about the shape of X the way you might expect. They are built around one strict rule, X must be a genuinely two dimensional array, shaped n_samples by n_features, even in the one feature case. That last part is where almost every beginner gets tripped up at least once.
4.1 Why X Must Be Genuinely Two Dimensional

When you select more than one column from a DataFrame, pandas gives you back another DataFrame, and calling .to_numpy() on it produces a proper 2D array without you having to think about it, because there is more than one column to arrange side by side. Select a single column instead, and pandas gives you back a Series, one dimensional by nature. Convert that to a NumPy array and you get a 1D array, shape (n,), not the (n, 1) that scikit-learn actually wants.

code.content:
X_single = df["sqft"].to_numpy()
print(X_single.shape)   # (4,)  one dimensional, just a flat list of numbers

# passing this straight into a scikit-learn model raises something like:
# ValueError: Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead

blocks.alt: Why X Must Be Genuinely Two Dimensional
blocks.caption: The single most common beginner error in this entire pipeline.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706763-999269791.png

blocks.title: Reading the actual error
blocks.content: scikit-learn error messages are unusually helpful here. If you ever see "Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead", that is the library telling you exactly this problem, and its suggested fix is almost always the reshape pattern covered next.

blocks.text: 4.2 The reshape(-1, 1) Fix

You already know how reshape works from the earlier Reshaping lesson, the same buffer of numbers gets reinterpreted into a new shape, as long as the total element count still matches, and -1 tells NumPy to work out one of the dimensions automatically instead of you computing it by hand. This section is really just that same tool applied to one very specific, very common situation.

reshape(-1, 1) means exactly this: the 1 fixes the second dimension at exactly one column, that part is not negotiable, you are explicitly asking for a single feature column. The -1 then tells NumPy, whatever number of rows makes the element count work out, figure that out yourself. For a flat array of 4 numbers, NumPy works out that -1 must mean 4 rows, so the result comes out shaped (4, 1), genuinely two dimensional, exactly one column, exactly what scikit-learn expects.

blocks.caption: One reshape call turns a rejected shape into an accepted one.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706765-941948487.png

blocks.caption: Two arguments, two jobs, negative one infers, one fixes.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706765-610111663.png

code.content:
X_single = df["sqft"].to_numpy()
print(X_single.shape)            # (4,)

X_single = X_single.reshape(-1, 1)
print(X_single.shape)            # (4, 1)  now ready to fit

blocks.title: A reshape trap worth remembering
blocks.content: It is easy to write reshape(1, -1) by accident instead of reshape(-1, 1). That produces a single row with every value squeezed into it as separate columns, shape (1, n), the opposite of what you want. When in doubt, read it out loud as it is written, negative one rows inferred, one column fixed, and double check the printed shape before moving on.

blocks.text: 5. Reassembling Arrays: column_stack and hstack

Real preprocessing pipelines rarely process every column the same way in one single step. A numeric column might go through scaling, a categorical column might go through one hot encoding, a binary flag might need nothing more than a reshape. Each of those steps can leave you holding a separate NumPy array, and at the very end you need to glue them all back together, side by side, into one final X matrix before training. That gluing step is exactly what np.column_stack() and np.hstack() are for.

blocks.caption: Three separately processed pieces, one final matrix.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706766-463155878.png
5.1 np.column_stack for Combining Columns

np.column_stack() was built specifically for this job. Give it a list of arrays, and it lines each one up as a column in the result. If you hand it 1D arrays, it treats each one as a single column automatically, which is exactly the behavior you want when reassembling separately processed features.

code.content:
import numpy as np

scaled_sqft = np.array([0.1, 0.8, -1.1, 1.5])
scaled_distance = np.array([-0.4, 1.2, -0.9, 2.0])
garage_flag = df["has_garage"].to_numpy() if "has_garage" in df else np.array([1, 0, 0, 1])

X_combined = np.column_stack([scaled_sqft, scaled_distance, garage_flag])
print(X_combined.shape)   # (4, 3)  three 1D arrays became three columns

blocks.text: 5.2 column_stack Versus hstack on 1D Arrays

np.hstack() is the more general purpose horizontal stacking function, and it is genuinely useful, but it treats 1D arrays differently than column_stack does. Given two 1D arrays, hstack concatenates them end to end into one longer 1D array, it does not turn them into columns. Given 2D arrays with matching row counts, hstack lines them up side by side just like column_stack does. The two functions only disagree on the 1D case, which happens to be exactly the case you run into constantly when reassembling individually processed feature columns.

code.content:
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
b = np.array([5, 6, 7, 8])

print(np.hstack([a, b]).shape)         # (8,)    concatenated end to end
print(np.column_stack([a, b]).shape)   # (4, 2)  each array became a column

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","np.column_stack","np.hstack"],"rows":[["Built for","Stacking 1D arrays as columns of a 2D result","General horizontal concatenation"],["Input is 1D arrays","Each array becomes its own column automatically","Arrays are concatenated end to end into one longer 1D array"],["Input is 2D arrays","Stacks along the second axis","Also stacks along the second axis, identical to column_stack here"],["Safer default for feature reassembly","Yes, behaves correctly regardless of input dimensionality","Only if you are certain every input is already 2D"]]}

blocks.title: The practical takeaway
blocks.content: When you are reassembling processed feature columns and are not one hundred percent sure every array is already 2D, reach for np.column_stack(). It gives you the column behavior you actually want whether the inputs are 1D or 2D, while hstack silently does something different depending on what it receives.

blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: DataFrame to Model Ready Arrays

Time to put every piece from this lesson together in order, starting from a small preprocessed housing DataFrame and ending with arrays a model would genuinely accept. Watch the shape printed after every single step, that is the habit worth building, never assume a shape, always confirm it.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "sqft": [1200, 1450, 900, 1600, 1100],
    "bedrooms": [3, 3, 2, 4, 2],
    "has_garage": [1, 0, 0, 1, 1],
    "distance_to_city_km": [5.2, 12.8, 3.1, 20.4, 7.7],
    "price": [62, 71, 48, 88, 55],
})

# Step 1: the X and y split, a shape level split done before anything else
feature_cols = ["sqft", "bedrooms", "has_garage", "distance_to_city_km"]
X = df[feature_cols].to_numpy()
y = df["price"].to_numpy()

print("X shape:", X.shape)   # (5, 4)  five rows, four feature columns, genuinely 2D
print("y shape:", y.shape)   # (5,)    five target values, a plain 1D array

# Step 2: a model trained on sqft alone needs that single column reshaped
X_single = df["sqft"].to_numpy()
print("before reshape:", X_single.shape)   # (5,)   1D, rejected by scikit-learn
X_single = X_single.reshape(-1, 1)
print("after reshape:", X_single.shape)    # (5, 1) 2D, accepted by scikit-learn

# Step 3: reassembling two separately scaled columns with the garage flag
scaled_numeric = np.array([
    [0.1, -0.4],
    [0.8, 1.2],
    [-1.1, -0.9],
    [1.5, 2.0],
    [-0.3, 0.1],
])
garage_flag = df["has_garage"].to_numpy().reshape(-1, 1)
X_combined = np.column_stack([scaled_numeric, garage_flag])
print("combined shape:", X_combined.shape)   # (5, 3)  two scaled columns plus the flag column

blocks.alt: Worked Example: DataFrame to Model Ready Arrays
blocks.caption: Every shape confirmed, every array ready.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442706766-463250948.png

Notice that every print statement in that example exists purely to confirm a shape assumption before moving on. X came out (5, 4), a genuinely 2D array with one row per house and one column per feature. y came out (5,), a plain 1D array of prices. The single sqft column needed an explicit reshape before it matched what a model expects, and the three separately built arrays in step three combined cleanly into one (5, 3) feature matrix. That habit of checking .shape after every transformation is the single most useful debugging tool in this entire part of a pipeline.
7. Recap

items: Use .to_numpy() over .values in new code, it is explicit, accepts arguments, and always returns a genuine ndarray, even for tricky extension dtypes like Categorical or timezone aware datetimes
X is a 2D array of every feature column, shaped n_samples by n_features, y is a 1D array of just the target column, shaped n_samples
The X and y split is a shape level split done first, splitting columns into inputs and an answer, distinct from the row level train and test split covered next
A single feature column comes out of a DataFrame as 1D, and needs an explicit reshape(-1, 1) to become the 2D shape scikit-learn requires
reshape(-1, 1) means negative one infers the row count automatically, one fixes the column count at exactly one
np.column_stack() reliably reassembles separately processed 1D or 2D arrays into one final feature matrix, np.hstack() only matches that behavior once every input is already 2D
